titles.399: Annotatio II §.VIII open PERDURATIO: Seemed extinct — Waldenses not consub; revived by John of Paris
titles.400: Annotatio II §.VIII: Scotus and Durandus (1320) tolerate revival; Aquinas not to be dragged in
titles.401: Annotatio II §.VIII: Peter d’Ailly of Cambrai (1414) favors it — Luther admits drawing from him
titles.402: Annotatio II §.VIII: Luther’s Captivity — true bread and wine; Thomist opinions are not articles of faith
titles.403: Annotatio II §.VIII close: Bayer wastes oil proving Luther ≠ Cambrai; stop before §.IX Marburg

latin.399: §. VIII. Etsi verò hoc pacto extincta visa est Consubstantiatio, exiguo satis tempore & à paucioribus edocta; Waldensibus etiam (in quorum doctrina de S. Coena, Consubstantiationis subtilioris sententiam conservatam nonnulli gloriantur) diversum prorsus à Consubstantiatione profitentibus, id quod Annotatio nostra quarta ad oculum ostendet; tamen resuscitata quasi è mortuis postliminio fuit, sub finem Seculi supra dicti XIII., per Johannem Parisienfem, Monachum ex ordine Dominicano.
latin.400: Non-improbata Scholasticis nonnullis, sigillatim Scoto, subtili doctori, initio seculi XIV, famosissimoque Durando, Anno 1320, quorum testimonia lege apud Franciscum Foris Otrokocsi in Irenico Cap. 6. §. 27. & seq. non item Thomæ Aquinati, à Dorschæo, hoc locô, neutiquam in Consensum trahi merito, quanquam fassus introducatur Transsubstantiationem ex verbis Institutionis probari haud posse.
latin.401: Donec tandem Petrus de Aliaco Cardinalis Cameracensis, qui Concilii Constantiensis tempore floruit, cujusque manu & consiliis Johannes Hussus & Hieronymus Pragensis, Viri Dei Christique martyres, miserè periêre, initio Seculi XV. Anno scil. 1414. apertius illi favere cœpit, à quo etiam D. Lutherus eandem hausisse fatetur ipsemet Lib. de Captiv. Babyl. Tom. 2. Operum Latinorum Jenensium fol. 263.
latin.402: Dedit inquit, mihi quondam, cùm Theologiam Scholasticam haurirem, occasionem cogitandi, Cardinalis Cameracensis Libro sententiarum quarto acutissime disputans: Multò probabilius esse & minus superfluorum miraculorum poni, si in altari verus panis verumque vinum non autem sola accidentia esse astrurentur, nisi Ecclesia determinasset contrarium. Postea videns, quæ esset Ecclesia, quæ hoc determinasset, nempe Thomistica, hoc est Aristotelica, audacior factus sum & qui inter saxum & sacrum hærebam, tandem stabilivi conscientiam meam sententia priori: esse videlicet verum panem verumque vinum, in quibus Christi vera caro verusque sanguis non aliter nec minus sit, quam illi sub accidentibus suis ponunt. Quod feci, quia vidi, Thomistarum opiniones, sive probentur à Papa, sive à Concilio, manere opiniones, nec fieri articulos fidei, etiamsi Angelus de Cœlo aliud statueret. Nam quod sine scripturis asseritur aut revelatione probata, opinari licet, credi non est necesse &c.
latin.403: Unde non potest non oleum & operam perdere Bajerus, in id annisus, ut ostendat, Lutherum & diversam à Cameracensi opinionem, & præter Cameracensem, pluribus communem, fovisse, Disput. de Impan. num. 50.

pass_a.399: §. VIII. Although by this pact Consubstantiation seemed extinct — taught for a short enough time and by rather few; the Waldenses also (in whose doctrine of the Sacred Supper some boast a subtler Consubstantiation sentence preserved) professing something altogether different from Consubstantiation, which our fourth Annotation will show to the eye — yet it was resuscitated as if from the dead by right of return, toward the end of the aforesaid 13th Century, by John of Paris, a Monk of the Dominican order.
pass_a.400: Not disapproved by some Scholastics, especially Scotus the subtle doctor at the start of the 14th century, and the most famous Durandus in the year 1320 — whose testimonies read in Francis Foris Otrokocsi’s Irenicum ch. 6 §§.27ff. — not likewise Thomas Aquinas, who is by no means rightly dragged into Consent here by Dorsche, although he is introduced as having confessed Transubstantiation cannot be proved from the Institution words.
pass_a.401: Until at length Peter d’Ailly, Cardinal of Cambrai, who flourished at the time of the Council of Constance, and by whose hand and counsels John Huss and Jerome of Prague, men of God and Christ’s martyrs, miserably perished, at the start of the 15th Century, namely the year 1414, began more openly to favor it — from whom also Dr. Luther himself confesses he drew the same, in On the Babylonian Captivity Tom. 2 of the Jena Latin Works fol. 263.
pass_a.402: The Cardinal of Cambrai, he says, once gave me occasion for thinking when I was drinking Scholastic Theology, disputing most sharply in the fourth book of the Sentences: that it is much more probable and fewer superfluous miracles are posited if on the altar true bread and true wine, not mere accidents, were asserted, unless the Church had determined the contrary. Afterward seeing what Church it was that had determined this — namely the Thomist, that is Aristotelian — I grew bolder, and who hung between the rock and the sacred, at length I stabilized my conscience in the prior sentence: namely that there is true bread and true wine, in which Christ’s true flesh and true blood are no otherwise nor less than they place under their accidents. Which I did because I saw Thomists’ opinions, whether approved by Pope or Council, remain opinions and do not become articles of faith, even if an Angel from Heaven should establish otherwise. For what is asserted without Scriptures or proved revelation may be opined; it is not necessary to believe &c.
pass_a.403: Whence Bayer cannot but lose oil and labor, having strained to show that Luther fostered both an opinion diverse from the Cambrai [cardinal’s] and, besides Cambrai’s, one common to many — Disputation on Impanation no. 50.

399: §.VIII PERDURATIO: Consubstantiation looked extinct — short-lived, few teachers; Waldenses (some claim) keep a subtler line, but they actually teach something else (see Annotatio IV).
Yet it rose again near the end of the 13th century through John of Paris, Dominican.
400: Some Scholastics did not reject the revival — Scotus early in the 14th century, and Durandus in 1320 (Otrokocsi, Irenicum VI.27ff.).
Aquinas is not to be dragged into this consent by Dorsche, even if he grants Transubstantiation is not proved from the Institution words alone.
401: Peter d’Ailly, Cardinal of Cambrai, at Constance (1414) began to favor it more openly — the same whose hand and counsel saw Huss and Jerome of Prague perish.
Luther himself confesses he drew that line from Cambrai (Babylonian Captivity, Jena Latin II fol. 263).
402: Luther: Cambrai’s Sentences IV gave him leave to think true bread and wine on the altar likelier than bare accidents — unless the Church had ruled otherwise.
Seeing that Church was Thomist/Aristotelian, he fixed his conscience: true bread and wine, with Christ’s true flesh and blood no less than under accidents.
Thomist opinions stay opinions, not articles of faith — even if an angel from heaven said otherwise; without Scripture or proven revelation, opinion is free, belief not owed.
403: So Bayer wastes oil and labor trying to prove Luther both differed from Cambrai and shared a wider common opinion (Disput. de Impan. §50).
Stop before §.IX (Marburg determination; difficulties of corporal-in-bread presence).
